questions.q: What is a playbook, as this lesson defines it?
options: A defined, automated sequence of steps that runs whenever a specific type of alert triggers it
A manual checklist an analyst must complete without any automation
A list of every tool a SOC has purchased
A written policy document reviewed once a year
questions.explain: A playbook is the concrete, automated recipe that runs in response to a specific trigger.

questions.q: In the phishing-report playbook example, what happens after the sender and URLs are extracted?
options: The email is forwarded to every employee in the company
They're checked against threat intel feeds to determine if they're malicious
The email is immediately deleted with no further checks
The playbook ends without taking any further action
questions.explain: Enrichment -- checking the extracted indicators against threat intel -- comes next, before any branching decision.

questions.q: What does the playbook do if the sender/URL is confirmed malicious?
options: Auto-quarantines the email from every inbox it reached and notifies the reporting user
Sends the email back to the original sender
Immediately isolates every host in the company
Takes no action and closes the report
questions.explain: A confirmed-malicious verdict triggers an automatic quarantine across all affected inboxes, plus user notification.

questions.q: What two conditions does a scenario need to meet to be a good playbook candidate?
options: It must be repeatable (happens often enough to automate) and well-understood (every outcome's correct response is already known)
It must only ever involve one specific tool
It must require legal approval before every single run
It must be rare and poorly documented
questions.explain: Playbooks are safe to automate specifically because a human already worked out the correct response to every branch in advance.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say playbooks break down on genuinely novel incidents?
options: Playbooks are only designed for use by senior analysts
Novel incidents never generate any alerts in the first place
There's no pre-agreed decision tree for a situation nobody has faced before, risking a confident but wrong automated action
Novel incidents are actually easier to automate than routine ones
questions.explain: Without a known-correct response already worked out, an automated playbook action is a guess dressed up as confidence.
